VISION The vision for the Passenger Environment Program is designed to create a more coordinated and proactive approach to passenger-facing cleaning operations by aligning station services, cleaning operations, transit hubs, and bus shelter maintenance under a single operational framework.

OVERVIEW The Program adopts a unified operational approach that is focused on improving the cleanliness, appearance, safety, and overall customer experience across all MARTA passenger -facing facilities.
The Program centralizes key operational functions under a coordinated structure to ensure consistent service delivery, accountability, and rapid response to customer and operational needs.
The Program supports daily operations, special events of all sizes, and long term overall system appearance across rail stations, transit hubs, bus shelters, and surrounding passenger access areas.
The Program increases operational accountability, enhance coordination between internal teams and contractors, and utilize technology and performance metrics to improve service delivery.

i: A motion was made by Ms. Reynolds, seconded by Mr. Sinyard, and carried unanimously that the Committee recommend the Board adopt the Resolution to approve the Proposed Amendments to the Rules for Air Quality Control, Chapter 391-3-1.
Mr. Lambert called on James Boylan, Chief of the Air Protection Branch, to present action on Proposed Amendments to the Rules for Air Quality Control, Chapter 391-3-1 pertaining to Permit Fees.

Mr. Boylan stated these amendments require Georgia Environmental Protection Division (EPD), under the Federal Clean Air Act and the Georgia Air Quality Act, to collect sufficient revenue in the form of permit fees to fund the direct and indirect costs of the permitting program.
Mr. Boylan stated that Georgia’s current air permit fee structure includes three main categories for permit fees.
Mr. Boylan stated that annual fees and permit application fees for Fiscal Year 2025 will remain the same as the current fees and there are no changes proposed.

Mr. Boylan stated that there is a proposed rule change to revise the date that administrative fees start being calculated from the day after October 1, to the day following the first business day of September.
Mr. Boylan stated that there was one verbal, public comment and there were no written comments submitted.

i: Ms. Addison called on Jill Andrews, Chief of Coastal Management Section, Coastal Resources Division, for a briefing on the proposed new chapter to the Rules of the Department of Natural Resources Coastal Resources Division, Private Recreational Docks, Chapter 391-2-1.
Ms. Andrews stated the briefing is on the proposed new rule, 391-2-1, related to private docks.

Ms. Andrews stated the proposed new rule will establish standards and criteria for the regulation of private docks for recreational purposes in tidal waters, provided the applicant qualifies for the private dock exemption under the Coastal Marshlands Protection Act, under part 12-5-291 7 and 7.1 bec
Ms. Andrews stated that while generally not regulated under the CMPA, docks in coastal Georgia have been regulated by the US Army Corps of Engineers since at least 1979.
She added that Rule .05 is the main substance as this is where they set the size standards for new docks.
Ms. Andrews stated that to start, this rule will address docks accessing small waterways less than 20 ft. wide.
She further stated that these docks are limited to small pierheads as there is no room to put floats in the water and still maintain safe navigation.
She added that all docks must be 10 ft. off an extended property line or dock corridor.

Ms. Andrews stated that fixed walkways are limited to a maximum of 6 ft. width and may not exceed 1,000 ft. in length provided that the total square footage of the walkway does not exceed 3,000 sq. ft.
She further stated that the size here is capped at 300 sq. ft. which, again, has been the standard since 2012.

The Board adopted the Resolution to approve the Proposed Amendments to the Rules for Enhanced Inspection and Maintenance. The amendments include adding a Class IIIG public water system classification and creating a new groundwater certification.
i: A motion was made by Mr. Garcia, seconded by Mr. Hatfield, and carried unanimously that the Committee recommend the Board adopt the Resolution to approve the Proposed Amendments to the Rules for Enhanced Inspection and Maintenance, Chapter 391-3-20.

Ms. Truszczynski stated these amendments will add a Class IIIG public water system classification to accommodate a new drinking water operator license classification.

Ms. Truszczynski stated that the Board of Examiners was requested by water systems to create a new groundwater certification to help relieve the shortage of drinking water operators for groundwater only systems.

Ms. Truszczynski stated that in preparing the proposed amendments, EPD issued a public notice on September 28, 2023, conducted a public meeting on November 2, 2023, and accepted comments from the public through November 9, 2023.

Hall County millage rate is 15.544 mills and 14.50 mills after the LOST rollback.

i: Evaluating Content Use these 10 questions to evaluate the value your website content provides to your users.
1. Is the information presented up to date? If not, how can it be updated to be relevant for current times? If information is outdated, and can’t be updated, delete or archive it.
2. Is the information presented something customers are likely to look for on your site, or would they be more likely to do a general browser search?
For example, information on how to assemble a survival kit is something that customers are likely to search for and not expect to be provided by their city or county.
Leave information like this off the site or link to a verified source.
3. Does this information come from an authoritative source other than your organization (i.e., FEMA)?
If you are not the authority, provide a link to the authoritative source instead of repeating and maintaining the information on your own pages.
4. Is there sufficient contact information provided?

2022 Comprehensive Plan Hart County 1 INTRODUCTION 1 Purpose Planning is the act of looking toward the future, regarding the possibilities, and then choosing a particular course or set of actions in order to achieve a desired set of outcomes.
It is the art of deliberately choosing your actions based on a specific goal, be it a secure retirement, the most fulfilling trip, or a successful business venture.
Planning is how we achieve control over our fates, or at the least realize more of what we want, and less of what we don’t.
“Always plan ahead. It wasn’t raining when Noah built the ark.” Richard Cushing
The purpose of local government planning is to provide guidance for everyday decision-making by government officials and other community leaders.

The White County Board of Commissioners held a Budget Work Session on Thursday, May 7, 2026 at 8:30 a.m. in the Board Room at the Administration Building.

Present for the meeting were: Chairman Travis Turner, Commissioner Shan Ash, Commissioner Lyn Holcomb, Commissioner Edwin Nix, Commissioner Craig Bryant, County Manager Derick Canupp, Finance Director Jodi Ligon, Deputy Clerk Julie Johnson, and Assistant County Manager / Clerk Shanda Murphy.
Chairman Turner called the meeting to order.

He advised that information had been updated since the April 13, 2026 Budget Work Session and the purpose of the meeting today would be to provide staff with the final guidance needed in order to move forward with preparing the required advertisements for the budget public hearing and adoption.
Mr. Canupp presented the following information concerning the Fiscal Year 2027 General Fund Budget:

There was a consensus to move forward with the Anthem renewal option for employee insurance which included changing the health plan paid co-insurance from 100% to 90%, office visit co-pays from $25/$50 to $30/$60, and increasing employee premiums 8% - with the total county increase being $525,296.00
There was consensus to add a part-time mechanic to the Road Department’s budget, with plans to bring some of the basic maintenance of county vehicles in-house as a cost savings measure.
It was noted that with the elimination of the community service program expense in this departmental budget – there would not be an increase in the overall expense in order to add this.
a public hearing would be held for the budget on Monday, June 8, 2026 at :30 p.m.

http://www.athensclarkecounty.com/Agenda.s: The meeting took up discussions on affordable housing challenges in Athens-Clarke County, including rental market issues, homeownership trends, and the local housing system. i: First motion by Mayor Girtz, seconded by Rick Parker.
Rick Parker introduced Connie Staudinger as the new Executive Director of Athens Housing Authority, and Mayor Girtz announced that Commissioners Houle and Thornton have joined the committee.
Solomon Smothers provided updates about proposed 2023 GICH Point Process, and the 5/19/23 application deadline.

HR&A provided a recap of the discussion during 12/2/22 meeting, and introduced the day’s discussion focused on ACC’s 3 key primary housing challenges: lack of quality affordable rental homes, lack of support for homeownership, and a modest affordable housing delivery system.

HR&A presented findings to date and led discussion around the local rental housing market, including housing cost burden among renters, rental housing gap, typology and vacancy rates in subsidized and naturally occurring affordable rental units, and rent increases.
HR&A presented findings to date and led discussion on homeownership trends and challenges in ACC, including home prices, mortgage denials, housing stock and homeowner cost burden.

HR&A presented findings on local housing system, including strengths and areas of improvement like expanding/sustaining funding, building mission-driven affordable housing capacity, and sustaining the focus on affordable housing.

i: The Burke County Board of Commissioners met for a Called Meeting concerning Broadband on Tuesday, February 8, 2022, at 4:30 pm in the Commissioners Training Room at the Burke County Courthouse.

Manager Waldrop began by recognizing the Board of Commissioners, Burke County School Board, and Planters Telephone Coop as partners in applying for a state grant to supplement funds for broadband installation throughout Burke County.
Mr. Waldrop stated the County was unsuccessful in obtaining funding.

Steven Milner, CEO/GM, of Planters Telephone Cooperative, discussed the specifics on how each application was scored, stating Burke County’s application was strong and on par with other applications submitted.
Mr. Milner stated the RDOF assignment (Rural Digital Opportunity Fund) was most likely the biggest encumbrance in the denial.

Mr. Milner then stated that during the RDOF, the winning bids were submitted December 2020 and Planters was eliminated by a company that has not been approved by the FCC and since been dissolved and incapable of meeting its obligations to the Burke and Jefferson County markets.
Commissioner Evans inquired what can be done with the funding the County and Board of Education currently has available to get a start on obtaining broadband.

Mr. Milner stated the best opportunity is to understand there is still substantial funding coming through the State and Burke County may want to consider a larger funds match on their application to appear more desirable.

http://www.athensclarkecounty.com/Agenda.t: Unified Government of Athens-Clarke County Meeting Summary Meeting Name: ARPA Affordable Housing Advisory Committee (GIC
http://www.athensclarkecounty.com/Agenda.s: The meeting discussed the Affordable Housing Implementation Strategy (AHIS), including its recommendations to address housing challenges in Athens-Clarke County. The committee reviewed the current housing market conditions and the draft housing strategy, and HR&A outlined next steps for the public comment period and M&C vote in September. The AHIS does not include specific recommendations for rapid rehousing or homelessness strategies, but these will be addressed in a separate plan.
i: Alejandra Calva welcomed the committee and presented the day’s agenda.
The Committee did not vote on April meeting minutes because quorum was not met.

HR&A provided a recap of AHIS process and prior discussions with committee; then previewed the day’s agenda to include a review with the committee about the current housing market conditions, and the draft housing strategy.
HR&A provided a quick update on the next steps regarding the public comment period, culminating in M&C vote in September.
HR&A shared the three primary housing challenges in ACC: limited public funding allocated toward housing, lack of quality affordable rental homes, lack of support for local homeownership.

Specific to the three housing challenges, HR&A described 3 key recommendations to respond to ACC’s housing market: (a) identify the ongoing local public funding, (b) build and preserve quality affordable rental homes, and (c) expand access to homeownership and protect existing homeowners.

HR&A explained that ACCGov will have to rely more on subsidy programs to meet its housing goals, and less so on land use (as land is generally limited in ACC) and tenants’ rights (given state-level laws).

HR&A shared that the AHIS includes an implementation plan to deploy the recommended policies over the next few years, including: a. Immediate term (in process now): (a)Expand down payment assistance program, and (b) increase funding for owner-occupied repair programs b. Near-term (2023): (a) establi
There was a brief discussion about the need to use actual income figures vs. relying solely on AMI percentages, both in final plan and in related discussions.
HR&A recommended that ACCGov implement programs that support existing and prospective low- and moderate-income homeowners in Athens-Clarke County.

i: Chattahoochee Hills Barn Quilt Trail www.chatthillsbarnquilttrail.com Located just 30 minutes south of the world's busiest airport in Atlanta, Georgia, is a hidden gem of a small town called Chattahoochee Hills.
Untouched by sprawl and mega development, this community made an intentional decision to preserve its rural heritage when it incorporated in 2007.
The Chatt Hills Barn Quilt Trail was created in 2020 as a community art project to share the heritage of our city.
Each painted quilt is displayed on a building or barn, and each tells the story of the family and its history on the webpage’s Tour the Trail page (click on each barn quilt for its story.)
We invite you to take a self-guided tour by either following the suggested route below, or by creating your own route.
Visitors are welcome to take photos from the public road, and are invited to visit the local stores, businesses, and parks.

i: Welcome and Introductions Addie Weber, the Toole Design project manager, welcomed the group and reviewed the agenda, project team, and core team members responsibilities.
The core team consists of staff, elected and appointed officials, partner agencies, neighbors, and local businesses.

Its purpose is to 1) share community insight, 2) coordinate and collaborate with relevant partners, 3) give feedback on draft concepts, and 4) connect to team members’ networks to increase the project’s reach.

The Sugar Loop Greenway Master Plan (2016), the Sugar Hill SR 20 Corridor Study (2018), the Sugar Hill Downtown Master Plan LCI (2018), the GDOT SR 20 widening project, and the BUILD Grant application for a new pedestrian and bicycle bridge.
Several guiding principles for developing a signature trail were shared, based on previous plans and initial conversations with staff:

1. Designing a safe and comfortable facility for users of all ages and abilities; 2. Connecting community facilities and other useful destinations; 3. Maximizing access to nature; and 4. Using existing public land and right-of-way as much as possible.

The facility should be designed to attract and support a wide range of users, including people who fall into the “interested but concerned” group of bicyclist design user profiles and have higher standards for safety and comfort.
The opportunity to connect with local public transit options and facilitate multimodal travel behavior.

Others in attendance were Roger Lane, Mayor of Sardis; Jenny Johnson Sardis City Clerk; Kim Reddick, Girard City Clerk; William Cox, Mayor of Girard; Rosemary Baughman, Mayor of Vidette; Valerie Kirkland, Waynesboro City Manager; and Loriann Chancey, Blythe City Clerk.
Manager Waldrop initiated by discussing the 2020 Census figures and pointed out the County has grown approximately 5%, most being in the unincorporated areas.

Mr. Waldrop then gave an overview of the L. O. S. T.’s history and explained the distribution formulas that have been used since 1981 and stated there had been no change in the formula until 2012 when the City of Blythe was included in the formula, which was taken out of the County’s percentage.
Mr. Waldrop went on to explained that according to State law, for a city to qualify for L. O. S. T., they must provide three of the following six services and collect another form of tax.
The provided services are water, sewer, garbage collection, police, fire, and / or library.
Mr. Waldrop stated it is their duty to figure out a formula that is fair to all municipalities and there are three options.

The discussion centered on the Tourism Office transitioning from a Department of County Government to that of a Destination Marketing Organization (DMO), the specifics of which have yet to be determined.

Statistics included ~2200 visitors and ~$43 million generated by tourists in Oconee (up from $41million the year before).
Alex also reported that the Tourism Office had applied to the Georgia Department of Economic Development: Tourism office for the Tourism Product Development grant to renovate the Welcome Center.

http://www.lumpkincounty.gov/DocumentCen.s: The meeting discussed baseball rules for ages 7 and 8. It decided that games will consist of 6 innings. No new inning may begin after 1 hour 20 minutes or at any point in which mathematical elimination applies.
i: Baseball Rules – Ages 7 and 8 1. Games will consist of 6 innings. No new inning may begin after 1 hour 20 minutes or at any point in which mathematical elimination applies.
2. Three outs per inning or a five-run limit.
3. Coach will pitch to the batters. If pitch is illegal (per Dizzy Dean rules) it will be called a dead ball and counted against the batter as one of the five pitches.
a. There will be a twenty-foot arc in front of home plate. The ball must be on or past this line to be a fair ball (otherwise it is considered foul).
b. Pitching mound will be at 46 feet with a 10 foot, in diameter, circle.
c. A pitching line will be drawn from the 20-foot arc to the front of the 10-foot circle. The coach may pitch from any distance along this line.
d. One defensive coach will be added behind the catcher.
4. There is no infield fly rule.

i: Finance Director Wes Geddings reviewed the proposed 2019 millage and property rate increase as advertised in the legal organ of the County on July 25, 2019 and August 1, 2019.
The first Public Hearing was held on August 6, 2019, and the second Public Hearing was held at 11:00 a.m. on August 27, 2019.
Mr. Geddings stated that the Oconee County was proposing adoption of a millage rate of 6.686 (unincorporated) and 7.626 (incorporated).
The Property Digest reflects an increase due to an increase in assessed property values of $133,366,603.00.
The resulting Tax Digest countywide is $2,145,653,423.00.
Due to the increase in assessed property values, the proposed county millage rates are considered by state law to be tax increases of approximately 6.46% (unincorporated) and 7.93% (incorporated).
The increases result in the addition of $1.357 million to the Tax Digest.
The rollback rate increase is 0.406 mill (unincorporated) and 0.560 mill (incorporated).

i: The Commissioner adopted Resolution R-2026-43 to set the 2026 Millage Rate for Union County’s maintenance and operation at 3.842 mils.
The gross maintenance and operation millage rate for Union County was set at 6.018 for 2026 and was then decreased by 2.176 from the Local Option Sales Tax or LOST as it is most often referred to.
This gives a total millage rate for 2026 of 3.842 which is a decrease from last year’s millage rate of 3.952.
LOST is 1 cent on every dollar that is spent in Union County and is collected as part of Sales Tax.
This money is then given back to Union County after the State collects it for the sole purpose of offsetting property taxes.

http://peachtree-city.org/DocumentCenter.t: City Council of Peachtree City Workshop Meeting Minutes October 4, 2011 The Mayor and Council of the City of Peachtree C
i: City Manager Jim Pennington noted that there would only be one item for discussion that evening, the discussion of private streets.

City Engineer Dave Borkowski gave an overview of the issue, noting that Peachtree City had 22 single-family and multi-family residential neighborhoods (including condominiums but excluding apartments) with streets that were privately owned by the respective Home Owner Associations (HOAs).
The City’s Land Development Ordinance prohibited the construction of any additional private streets in single-family residential neighborhoods as of January 3, 2008.

The ordinance also indicated that, if a neighborhood so desired, they had the right to petition the City to take over the private streets through a formal request signed by all co-owners of the street, and they had to deed the right-of-way to the City and revise the final plat.
Borkowski said all ordinance requirements for the streets would also have to be met. That requirement had prevented any petitions from proceeding to date.
The specifications included 50 feet of right-of-way, cul-de-sacs with adequate right-of-way, maximum and minimum grade design, and a 22-foot pavement width.
Borkowski then used the Village Park neighborhood as an example of the difficulties in meeting the requirements.

The neighborhood had streets in a 46-foot utility and ingress-egress easement. To meet the City standards, the right of way would encroach into the yards, meaning the building setbacks (previously based on the curb) then extended into the existing homes.
Another resident asked, if the property was turned over in top-notch condition, if it could be considered starting from scratch.
A lot of the HOAs were getting behind in maintenance due to the economy, with members getting behind in their dues leading to less maintenance.

The motion to approve the budget passed unanimously. The City Manager presented a draft design for the Garrard Park playground.
i: Commissioner Robinson made a motion to approve the 2026 CDBG Action Plan budget, and Commissioner Brock seconded the motion.
Molly Majestic presented the 2026 Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) Annual Action Plan.
She reported that the City has received an allocation of $385,040 from HUD and that the budget for the upcoming year has been finalized.

Majestic noted that this amount is lower than last year’s allocation of approximately $415,000, but the department is appreciative of the funding given the overall reductions to the HUD program nationwide.
She explained that most of the budget cuts will affect public facilities and park improvements.

The proposed allocations for 2026 are as follows: • $215,040 for public facilities and park improvements, which must be located within a Qualified Census Tract (QCT). • $95,000 for the ongoing owner-occupied housing rehabilitation program. • $75,000 for general grant planning and administration.
City Manager Sammy Rich presented the newly received draft design for the planned Garrard Park playground.

https://www.romega.gov/AgendaCenter/View.s: The meeting discussed the current contract with Cliff Drysdale Management and the possibility of the City of Rome taking over management of the Rome Tennis Center. The committee approved a motion to let the contract expire and for the City to assume management. The City would take over the facility, and the current manager, Colt Gaston, would become a City employee.
i: Motion: Commissioner Collins made a motion to allow the current contract with Cliff Drysdale Management to expire, and for the City of Rome to assume management of the Rome Tennis Center.
Lisa Smith began by explaining to the committee that the 5-year contract with Cliff Drysdale Management, a subsidiary of Troon, expires on November 1, 2026.

Smith provided background on the facility's management history, noting that after the closure and staffing disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the City issued an RFP and entered into a management agreement with CDM in 2021.
Under the current agreement, the City pays CDM a $10,000 monthly management fee, in addition to covering facility expenses, employee salaries, and capital costs.

Smith noted that General Manager Colt Gaston, currently a CDM employee, has been central to the facility's success, including growth in tournament hosting and a doubling of economic impact over five years.
She stated that if the City does not renew the CDM contract, Gaston would transition to a City of Rome employee, along with the facility's other staff.

http://www.oconeecounty.com/AgendaCenter.s: The meeting discussed economic development history in Georgia, highlighting higher education, ports, and Hartsfield Jackson International Airport as key assets. It outlined the two main elements of economic development—new business recruitment and business retention—and the four parts of a successful plan: leadership, strategy, community development, and marketing. The group was tasked with considering suitable business sectors for Oconee County for the next meeting.
i: Craig Lesser, Pendleton Group, began the meeting by outlining economic development (ED) history in Georgia.
He mentioned that Georgia is home to three main divers in regard to ED: higher education, the ports and Hartsfield Jackson International Airport.
Craig also mentioned that ED is a team effort. It takes collaboration to work effectively.
Craig shared that there are two main elements to ED, new business recruitment and business retention.
Craig outlined the four parts of a successful ED plan: leadership, strategy, community development and marketing.
He then discussed several Oconee specific statistics regarding education, income, employment, etc.
Craig then opened the floor to the taskforce members who were able to share what they thought were Oconee’s strengths, weaknesses and/or a vision for the future.
After discussion, Craig tasked the group to prepare for the next meeting by thinking of what types of business/industry sectors would fit in Oconee.

http://www.oconeecounty.com/AgendaCenter.s: The meeting discussed economic development history in Georgia, highlighting higher education, ports, and Hartsfield Jackson International Airport as key assets. It outlined the two main elements of economic development—new business recruitment and business retention—and the four parts of a successful plan: leadership, strategy, community development, and marketing. The group was tasked with considering suitable business sectors for Oconee County for the next meeting.
i: Craig Lesser, Pendleton Group, began the meeting by outlining economic development (ED) history in Georgia.
He mentioned that Georgia is home to three main divers in regard to ED: higher education, the ports and Hartsfield Jackson International Airport.
Craig also mentioned that ED is a team effort. It takes collaboration to work effectively.
Craig shared that there are two main elements to ED, new business recruitment and business retention.
Craig outlined the four parts of a successful ED plan: leadership, strategy, community development and marketing.
He then discussed several Oconee specific statistics regarding education, income, employment, etc.
Craig then opened the floor to the taskforce members who were able to share what they thought were Oconee’s strengths, weaknesses and/or a vision for the future.
After discussion, Craig tasked the group to prepare for the next meeting by thinking of what types of business/industry sectors would fit in Oconee.

Council reviewed guidance on developing clear and impactful Vision and Mission statements.

It was noted that a Vision Statement should be a single sentence communicating desired goals, aspirations, and overall impact, while a Mission Statement should outline what the city does, why it does it, and how it serves the community.
Discussion emphasized that both statements should engage all stakeholders and serve as a unifying call to action rather than simply identifying governmental functions.

Flemington’s current Mission Statement was reviewed and determined to focus primarily on governmental operations ("develop and administer policies") rather than reflecting the broader purpose and identity of the city as a whole.
The current motto, "Preserving our heritage. Shaping our future.", was also reviewed.

i: Minutes of Public Hearing Elbert County Board of Commissioners Wednesday, August 30, 2017 12:00 p.m. The Elbert County Board of Commissioners held a Public Hearing on a tentatively adopted millage rate that will require an increase in property taxes by 4.25% in the unincorporated portion of the coun
This is the first of three public hearings that are required by law.
Chairman Lyon stated that the public hearing is to hear from concerned citizens regarding a millage rate increase for economic development.
The reason being that Economic Development millage funds go into the Elbert County general fund and is designated for that purpose.
The hospital millage rate portion goes directly to the hospital therefore, by law, it is not necessary to have a public hearing on that millage rate increase.

He stressed the portion of the millage rate increase for economic development is not necessarily for construction of a spec building; but to build up funds to allow for incentives for companies that may want to locate here, infrastructure, roads and possibly land purchases.

Minutes of Public Hearing Elbert County Board of Commissioners Wednesday, August 30, 2017 6:00 P.M. This is the second of three public hearings to be held for a tentatively adopted millage rate increase for economic development.

Chairman Lyon again stated to those in attendance as he did at the earlier meeting; the money for economic development is not necessarily for a spec building but for engineering studies, site plans, purchase of property and other marketing strategies to help grow jobs.

https://www.cityofflemington.org/documen.s: The meeting took up a public hearing on the millage rate for the City of Flemington. The Council confirmed that the millage rate was to maintain current services and to grow, including the need for a larger city hall, parks and recreation, and eventually a police and fire department. The public hearing adjourned after no further comments or questions were received.
i: MPT Edwards welcomed all attendees and shared some quick expectations of decorum for a productive public hearing.
MPT Edwards gave a presentation regarding the reasons for the necessity of a millage rate to be enacted in order to balance the budget and provide services to the citizens.
After the presentation concluded, the MPT opened the floor to public comment and asked if any member of the audience in attendance wished to speak.

The overwhelming majority of comments were centered around homeowners’ associations, a few general questions about special fund revenues (and allowable usages), and one question about the city having its own police department.

The Council reconfirmed that the millage rate was to maintain current services and to grow; citing the need for a much larger city hall, parks and recreation, and eventually standing up a Flemington police and fire department.
With no other public comments or questions regarding the proposed millage rate, the public hearing adjourned at 6:25 p.m.

The County Manager then explained two options for distribution of the proceeds.
The first option was to leave the formula the same as the last time.

i: Sheriff Williams addressed the Board concerning the operations of the Detention Center, referencing a letter submitted to all Commissioners.

Sheriff Williams stated the Detention Center was over thirty years old, not designed for housing female inmates, lacks sufficient space to provide adequate safety and security for inmates and employees, and needs a larger medical ward.
Sheriff Williams reiterated once again the difficulty in recruiting and retaining employees and the working conditions are a factor.

Sheriff Williams then cited the improvements in services such as increased meal options, computers, educational services and computer usage and facilities operations that have occurred since taking office and stated they have been provided to improve inmate and employee safety.

According to the Sheriff, the Georgia Sheriff’s Association conducted a study on the detention center and rated the facility as inadequate and unsafe as it is not handicapped accessible, and stated several contractors stated it would be less costly to tear down and rebuilt then to modify the existin
The Sheriff stated the Burke County Grand Jury toured the facility and notified the District Attorney of the insufficiencies.
Sheriff Williams reminded the Board there was currently $1.5 million set aside for jail renovations and $2.5 million in the 2024-2030 SPOLST.

It was suggested that the County prepare a letter to the Chief Judge and District Attorney regarding the inmate population and need for cases to move forward towards adjudication and for the Sheriff to contact neighboring counties to provide housing for inmate overflow.

i: The Burke County Board of Commissioners met for a work session to discuss Solid Waste Collection

Manager Waldrop opened by stating he had provided the Board with copies of the collection proposals previously submitted, a manned convenience center cost analysis for 1, 5, and 10 sites, and a county comparison survey
Discussion began by evaluating use of poly carts for curbside service, manned / unmanned convenience centers, or a mixture of services
Discussion continued around manned convenience center sites and if the population would be better served with fewer collection sites and the additional costs of maintaining the sites
James Lanier, Ryland Environmental, and Brad Bowman, Atlantic Waste, offered their suggestions on what would best benefit the county based on their understanding of needs
Manager Waldrop informed the Board their options were to put the services back out to bid or choose a company from the already submitted bids and renegotiate service costs
Consensus was to individually look at submitted proposals and choose a company to move forward with to renegotiate terms
A Called Meeting was then set for November 16, 2022 at 4:00 pm for decision

https://www.burkecounty-ga.gov/Document%.t: BURKE COUNTY BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS CALLED MEETING – HEPHZIBAH ANNEXATION OCTOBER 16, 2026 The Burke County Board of Com
https://www.burkecounty-ga.gov/Document%.s: The meeting discussed the proposed annexation of certain parcels in Burke County by the City of Hephzibah, including the city's growth plans, water system expansion, and financial implications. It also addressed concerns about the loss of LOST and SPLOST revenues and explored alternatives such as intergovernmental agreements. The meeting concluded without taking any formal action on the annexation proposal.
i: Chair Martin explained that representatives of the City of Hephzibah Commission would present an overview of the proposed annexation, followed by an opportunity for public questions and comments.

Mr. Buchwitz provided an overview of the City of Hephzibah’s growth and water system expansion, noting that discussions with Burke County regarding annexation date back to the late 1980s and early 1990s.
Mr. Buchwitz stated that the City of Hephzibah’s 2018 Comprehensive Plan includes provisions for expanding its water system into Burke County.
Mr. Buchwitz explained that the City of Hephzibah would require control over water usage and development, necessitating annexation of the proposed service area.

Mr. Buchwitz explained the contiguity requirements for annexation into the City of Hephzibah, stating that nine (9) parcels in Burke County have expressed interest in annexation, with an additional seven (7) parcels having submitted petitions for annexation.
Mr. Buchwitz stated that the City of Hephzibah has not levied municipal property taxes since the 1970s and funds its operations through Richmond County LOST/SPLOST revenues and investment income.

Chair Martin expressed concerns regarding the proposed annexation, stating that water system expansion could be accomplished through an intergovernmental agreement between Burke County and the City of Hephzibah without the need for annexation.

Discussion between the Boards continued regarding the potential loss of LOST and TSPLOST revenues resulting from the proposed annexation, with concerns expressed that such losses could place an additional financial burden on Burke County and its existing municipalities and communities.
Mr. Ed Templeton requested a map of the area affected by the proposed annexation, which the County displayed for public viewing.
He inquired about the number of households that could potentially be served by the proposed water line expansion.

https://worthcountyboc.com/AgendaCenter/.s: The meeting discussed a presentation on Worth County’s retirement plan, including an in-service retirement option for employees reaching age 65 with five years of vesting. It also covered the county’s eligibility for GTIB funding for road resurfacing and the health insurance plan’s medical case manager service. The meeting addressed the requirement for employees to participate in case manager guidance and the matter of moving the evidence room versus building a new one.
i: Presentation A. Ron Rowe - ACCG Mr. Rowe said he met with Worth County employees every quarter to discuss their retirement plans.

Recently, a question arose that needed further explanation. He explained that Worth County’s plan contained an in-service retirement option for employees reaching age 65 with at least five years of vesting.

This employee could elect to begin receiving their retirement benefits and continue to work without a break in service. The change would be that this employee would still have to contribute 3% to the defined benefit plan but, his or her pension benefit would not increase as opposed to employees not

Mr. Rowe further explained that if an employee decided to retire and then come back to work for the County, the County could rehire that employee as long as the employee understood that their rehire was not guaranteed when they left.
In fact, when an employee retires, they must sign a “Bonafide Termination” form stating there was no conversation prior to retirement to rehire the retiree.
Mr. Rowe commended the Board for implementing this modest pension plan for their employees when one did not exist previously.
Discussion Items A. Georgia Transportation Infrastructure Bank (GTIB) application Administrator said Worth County was eligible to apply for new GTIB funding.
He and others surveyed possible roads needing resurfacing that also qualified as a “connector road” eligible for this type of funding.
Administrator said that the employees’ health insurance plan includes providing a medical case manager for employees experiencing any long-term illness or injury.
The case manager helps the employee navigate the insurance process and provides the employee with information on additional options or alternatives to their care.

i: First Public Hearing – Resolution 22-012 – To adopt the Fiscal Year 2023 Annual Budget.
Property Tax is a top revenue source for general community service operations.
The proposed budget for Fiscal Year 2023 the property tax is based on keeping the millage rate at 3.264 mills.

General fund expenditure changes include planned increases for current personnel, an addition of six new positions in the following departments: Finance (1), Police (3), Planning (2) and an additional $825,000 transfer to capital projects for the community (road paving, stormwater, and sidewalk impr

The Government Finance Officer Association (GFOA) best practices recommend no less than a minimum of two months reserves of expenses, but our Council has elected a more conservative approach to maintain four- and one-half months reserve.
The Tax Allocation District projects include all the downtown developments such as the Market Pavilion, Park and Streetscaping Project and the Mitchell Street Improvements.
Overall, the City wide budget increased 5.13%. We recommend approval of Resolution 22-012 to adopt the FY2023 Annual Budget.

The audit was for the Republican Senate Race and the Democratic Lt. Governor Race.
One batch (7 ballots) of absentee by mail and one Election Day batch (353 ballots) were to be counted.
Lynn Telford and Anne Moon counted the Election Day batch while Lynda Garrison and Sharon Pruitt counted the absentee by mail batch.
The ballots were counted by each board member assigned to their respective batch.
The audit numbers matched the computer count with no discrepancies found in either batch.

https://www.flowerybranchga.org/Document.s: The meeting discussed adopting Ordinance 532 to set the Ad Valorem tax rate for 2017 and 2018, with a net millage rate of 3.264. The council considered whether to roll back the mill rate, with some members arguing the city should proceed with the rollback due to increased revenue from franchise fees, SPLOST, insurance, and LOST collections. The motion to approve Ordinance 532 was carried.
i: There was a motion made to approve the Consent Agenda as presented.
There was a motion made to approve Ordinance 532 to Fix the Ad Valorem Tax Rate for the City of Flowery Branch for the Tax Year 2017 and the Fiscal Year 2018.
Councilmember Monica Beatty stated that the past millage rates don’t matter and that we need to consider what Flowery Branch needs today.
Councilman Anglin inquired if Councilmember Beatty felt the extra $50,000 should be designated for a specific purpose.
Councilmember Beatty stated yes, that is what is needed such as our roads, drainage etc.

Councilman Richards gave an example and stated that there is a mile of road in his subdivision with 90 residents along that mile of road paying approximately $150.00 in taxes a year which amounts to $270,000 over 20 years.
Councilman Anglin asked if the council considered the infrastructure needs when they approved to use 60% of SPLOST for the new city hall project.
Councilman Mundy advised that the city has received more then what was estimated with increased insurance premiums and additional revenue from permitting.
The mill rate can be rolled back and the city can still accomplish what has been proposed in the budget.

The council motioned to adjourn the meeting.
i: Resolution 18-012 - To Adopt the Fiscal Year 2019 Annual Budget
Finance Director Alisha Gamble summarized the review of the mill rate as follows: The millage rate for the past 3 fiscal years has been the same at 3.264 mills.
This is an increase of 0.186 mills from the rollback rate of 3.078 mills. We are requesting to keep the millage rate the same for Fiscal Year 2019.
According to the Hall County Tax Assessors Office, the average fair market value of a home in our area is $225,000 which assessed at 40% of market value calculates to $293.76 per taxpayer.
This is an increase of $16.74 per taxpayer. 3.264 mills will generate $1,310,893 in tax revenue for the City to provide services for citizens of Flowery Branch.

Keeping the millage rate at 3.264 mills, new or improved properties are estimated to increase revenue by $142,953 and the reassessment of existing real property is estimated to increase revenue by $74,891.
What will the increase in revenue contribute to? • All departments will receive a 2% cost of living adjustment and 3% merit increase for a total of $71,261.

• Public Safety will add a new officer and vehicle for a total of $101,402. The $40,000 cost of the new vehicle includes all the required equipment needed to get the vehicle in operational use for the patrol.

http://www.jenkinscountyga.com/uploads/B.s: The meeting discussed the proposed sale of land to Cantsink Solar and considered deed restriction options to ensure cleanup and disposal requirements. i: The motion was seconded by Charlie Dempsey and approved by the board.

Hiller Spann made a motion to move forward with the sale of the property with a deed restriction, ensuring that the language is as restrictive as possible regarding cleanup and disposal requirements in order to protect the City under its current ordinances.

Discuss Solar Project - A called meeting of the Jenkins County Development Authority was held to discuss deed restriction options related to the proposed sale of land to Cantsink Solar, upon which solar panels will be installed.

The board discussed recommendations from the Development Authority’s attorney advising that a bond be required to cover the disposal and cleanup of the solar panels upon decommissioning of the project.
Ms. Underwood reported that she had spoken with the purchaser, who indicated he was not interested in moving forward with the purchase if a bond requirement was included.

Further discussion noted that the existing solar project located within the City of Millen and adjacent to the property proposed for sale is not covered by a bond, but instead is regulated under the City of Millen’s Solar Ordinance.

While the ordinance is somewhat vague, it does include a provision allowing the City to recover costs incurred for cleanup or removal of solar equipment from the property owner through legal means, should the City be required to undertake such cleanup.
Sandy Miller requested that the minutes reflect his concern regarding the City’s level of protection in the absence of a bonded cleanup requirement.

https://www.jenkinscountyga.com/uploads/.s: The meeting discussed the proposed sale of land to Cantsink Solar and considered deed restriction options to ensure cleanup and disposal requirements. The board approved a motion to move forward with the sale using a deed restriction that includes as restrictive language as possible regarding cleanup and disposal. Sandy Miller requested that the minutes reflect his concern regarding the City’s level of protection in the absence of a bonded cleanup requirement.
i: The motion was seconded by Charlie Dempsey and approved by the board.

Hiller Spann made a motion to move forward with the sale of the property with a deed restriction, ensuring that the language is as restrictive as possible regarding cleanup and disposal requirements in order to protect the City under its current ordinances.

Discuss Solar Project - A called meeting of the Jenkins County Development Authority was held to discuss deed restriction options related to the proposed sale of land to Cantsink Solar, upon which solar panels will be installed.

The board discussed recommendations from the Development Authority’s attorney advising that a bond be required to cover the disposal and cleanup of the solar panels upon decommissioning of the project.
Ms. Underwood reported that she had spoken with the purchaser, who indicated he was not interested in moving forward with the purchase if a bond requirement was included.

Further discussion noted that the existing solar project located within the City of Millen and adjacent to the property proposed for sale is not covered by a bond, but instead is regulated under the City of Millen’s Solar Ordinance.

While the ordinance is somewhat vague, it does include a provision allowing the City to recover costs incurred for cleanup or removal of solar equipment from the property owner through legal means, should the City be required to undertake such cleanup.
Sandy Miller requested that the minutes reflect his concern regarding the City’s level of protection in the absence of a bonded cleanup requirement.

https://worthcountyboc.com/AgendaCenter/.s: The meeting discussed a presentation on Worth County’s pension plan, including an in-service retirement option for employees reaching age 65 with five years of vesting. It also addressed the application for Georgia Transportation Infrastructure Bank funding for road resurfacing and discussed moving the evidence room and littering in rights-of-way. The board considered a start date of July 1st for services and reviewed health insurance provisions for long-term illness or injury.
i: Presentation A. Ron Rowe - ACCG Mr. Rowe said he met with Worth County employees every quarter to discuss their retirement plans.

Recently, a question arose that needed further explanation. He explained that Worth County’s plan contained an in-service retirement option for employees reaching age 65 with at least five years of vesting.

This employee could elect to begin receiving their retirement benefits and continue to work without a break in service. The change would be that this employee would still have to contribute 3% to the defined benefit plan but, his or her pension benefit would not increase as opposed to employees not

Mr. Rowe further explained that if an employee decided to retire and then come back to work for the County, the County could rehire that employee as long as the employee understood that their rehire was not guaranteed when they left.
In fact, when an employee retires, they must sign a “Bonafide Termination” form stating there was no conversation prior to retirement to rehire the retiree.
Mr. Rowe commended the Board for implementing this modest pension plan for their employees when one did not exist previously.
Discussion Items A. Georgia Transportation Infrastructure Bank (GTIB) application Administrator said Worth County was eligible to apply for new GTIB funding.
He and others surveyed possible roads needing resurfacing that also qualified as a “connector road” eligible for this type of funding.
Commissioner Hall reported that he and Commissioner Willis met with Poulan and Sumner officials and discussed the 911 dispatching services.
Commissioner Roberts suggested a start date of July 1st to coincide with the beginning of the fiscal year.

i: Tiffany made a Motion and Steve seconded.
Brooke Anderson presented a video about the construction phase of Russell Creek Reservoir on the Etowah Water and Sewer Authority (EWSA) owned land.

The reservoir project is designed to provide sufficient water to maintain drinking water supply for up to 126,000 people, including unallocated commercial and industrial uses, in the event of drought (based on 2008- 2009 worst on record drought).
Construction completion is scheduled for Jan. 2028. It will take about an year to fill.
The "Linda G. Townley Pavilion and Parkland" is scheduled to be completed by 2029.
Etowah Water & Sewer (not the USACE) will be responsible for reservoir and dam maintenance for a further 105 years.

Swinson highlighted the county’s newly created Building and Public Facilities Authority (PFA) as a key tool in the funding process.

Ms. Gamble reviewed both items together and summarized the following: The chart below shows the millage history for the City from 2003-2020.
Over the past 17 years, there were three periods of millage fluctuations: ➢ 2004 to 2005: increase from 1.81 to 2.837 for a total increase of 1.027 mills.
➢ 2013 to 2014: increase from 2.837 to 3.337 for a total increase of 0.50 mills. ➢ 2015 to 2016: decrease from 3.337 to 3.264 for a total decrease of 0.073 mills
➢ From fiscal year 2016-2020 the City’s millage rate has been 3.264 mills. Staff is recommending 3.264 mills for fiscal year 2020.
➢ According to the Hall County Tax Assessors Office, the average fair market value of a home in our area is $250,000 which assessed at 40% of market value calculates to $326.40 per taxpayer.
This is an increase of $8.60 per taxpayer. 3.264 mills will generate $1,421,465 in tax revenue for the City to provide services for citizens of Flowery Branch.

https://dodgecountyga.com/wp-content/upl.s: The meeting discussed efforts to acquire land between Bleckley and Dodge counties to foster growth and secure a grant for water infrastructure. The meeting addressed the courthouse construction project and the role of financial advisors in securing the best interest rates for bonds.
i: Chairman McCranie gave the floor to Bleckley County Commissioner Mike Davis for an update from the Joint Development Authority of Bleckley and Dodge County.
Commissioner Davis discussed efforts to acquire land between the counties to foster growth and secure a grant for water infrastructure.
Commissioner Watkins provided an update from the Dodge County-Eastman Development Authority stating that a $2 million grant had been acquired to upgrade a 70-acre grad site at the airport.
Senator Walker stated that the grant was part of a rural site development initiative by Governor Kemp, and the DCEDA was awarded the maximum amount possible.
Commissioner Watkins discussed a 280-acre chip mill site with double rail spurs, which the DCEDA hopes to get grad certified.

Commissioner Flanagan discussed the courthouse construction project whereby the county would like to have new judicial and administrative buildings, as renovating the old courthouse would be costly, functionally inefficient, and difficult to make ADA-compliant.
Senator Walker noted there was a potential purchase of 165-acres adjacent to the public fishing area for enlarging the public fishing area through the DNR.
Financial Advisors Ricardo Cornejo and Courtney Rogers explained their role as fiduciaries who represent the county's interests in securing the best interest rates for bonds.

The meeting also included practicing escape plans through fire drills and explaining how to safely exit a room if the door is hot.
i: Home Escape Planning In a home fire, you may have only 2-3 minutes to get everyone out safely. Having working smoke alar
Here are some simple steps that you can take to prepare for a fire in your home should it happen: • Sit down with your family and draw a map or floor plan or your home.
Show all windows and doors. Show the location of each smoke alarm. Discuss these escape routes with each family member.
• Establish a meeting place outside your home. This can be a mailbox, tree, stop sign or anything else permanent.
The entire household should know to go to this spot in case of an emergency escape from the house. That way the entire household can be accounted for.
• Practice the plan – have fire drills at home, at least twice a year. o Push the button on the smoke alarm so everyone will know what sound it makes.
When the button is pushed, everyone should pretend it is a real fire and practice the escape plan. o Crawl low on the floor, even if you don’t see any smoke.
Feel the door to the bedroom if it is closed. Feel around the frame and the knob. If it is hot, don’t open it. Use the second way out.

https://www.gordoncountyga.gov/AgendaCen.s: The meeting discussed the history of the local arch and two historical monuments, and the condition of the 100-year-old statues, which are dangerously unstable. It also addressed the evaluation of the statues by a specialist and the conflicting ownership information for the property. The meeting approved the discussion and adjourned.
i: Jim Weaver made motion to approve; seconded by Valerie Robbins.
City Council Update: Jeff Henderson and Add Layson met with the city council to discuss the history of the local arch and its two historical monuments, located at Hwy 225/Hwy 41.
Statue Condition: Jeff reported that the 100-year-old statues, are dangerously unstable, and are currently held on by only two to three aging bolts.
Repair Logistics: A specialist from the Scott David Company in Chattanooga evaluated the statues.
Property Ownership: Research into historic deeds shows conflicting information about who owns the property the arch sits on (State DOT, US Government, or the Women’s Club).
